## 2

You don't need to trust NASA — you can test it yourself. Watch a ship cross the horizon: hull disappears first, masts last. That only happens on a curve. Every lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow on the moon is round; a flat disk would sometimes cast a line. Southern-hemisphere flights — Sydney to Santiago, ~11,000 km — make no sense on a flat map. And the cover-up would require every space agency on Earth, thousands of amateur balloon photographers, and the entire GPS system lying flawlessly for seventy years. People are terrible at keeping secrets. The sphere is simply what's there.

## 3

Here's the trick: the sky isn't blue — the *light* is. Sunlight looks white, but it's really all the colors mixed together, and air molecules scatter some of it sideways as it passes through the atmosphere. They don't scatter the colors equally, though. Blue light has short, tight waves, and short waves get knocked off course far more easily than the long, lazy waves of red light. So blue gets bounced all over the sky, and whichever direction you look, some of that scattered blue lands in your eye. The red mostly travels straight through.

Bonus: this is why sunsets are red. When the sun is low, its light cuts through much more air, and nearly all the blue gets scattered away en route. What survives the trip is red.

Second bonus: you might ask why the sky isn't *violet*, since violet scatters even more than blue. Two reasons — the sun emits less violet, and your eyes barely register it anyway.

## 4

雨是傍晚开始下的，起初只是屋檐上零星的滴答，到了夜里便连成了片。街上空了，路灯把积水照成一块一块的碎银。我坐在窗前听雨，偶尔有车碾过积水，哗的一声，像潮水漫过来又退下去。对面的楼只剩几扇窗还亮着，昏黄的光被玻璃上的雨水晕开，模糊成一团暖色。夜越来越深，雨还在下，世界安静得只剩这一种声音。
